Opinion: Does shampoo ruin the environment?
By David Robinson
We have a shampoo problem.
At least, we are about to, according to one of the biggest global brands, Unilever.
The company announced its plan to cut the use of plastic packaging in all of its products by 2025. But the details are sparse. Just how, exactly, the move to be achieved - particularly while maintaining the quality of some of the company's best-known consumer brands?
Shampoo is used in large quantities. In 2018, over 16bn individual pots of the stuff were dispensed by UK retailers and over two-thirds of consumers in the country admitted that they washed their hair every day. That was the case in America too. And across the Channel, many consumers use up to six different products when it comes to their weekly hair and beauty routines.
Shampoos help keep hair looking clean and healthy, but they often require individual cans, bottles and other disposable packaging which is not easily recycled. The company says it is committed to reducing packaging across all its brands and finding a more environmentally-friendly alternative.
In September, Unilever unveiled ambitious plans to turn 100% of its plastic packaging into recyclable, reusable, or compostable plastics and papers by 2025.
The company is trying to cut out plastic where possible - using paper-based materials in water-based formulations in a bid to reduce the number of cans, bottles, sachets and tubs that it puts on shelves each year.
